faqs.answer: A levain is a small batch of starter built for one bake, while your starter is the culture you keep alive from week to week. You take a spoonful of starter, feed it flour and water, and let it ripen into the levain the recipe needs. The starter stays in the jar, the levain goes in the dough.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a levain and a starter?

faqs.answer: A 1:5:5 build takes longer to ripen, which is exactly what an overnight build needs: mix it in the evening and it is ready in the morning. A 1:1:1 build peaks in a few hours and would be past its best by morning. The Perfect Loaf's levain builds at 1:2:2 ripen in about 5 hours at 74 to 76°F, which is a useful guide for timing.
faqs.question: Which ratio is best for an overnight levain?

faqs.answer: Yes, if it is ripe and at its peak, and the weight is right. A levain is just starter that was fed on a schedule. If your starter is bubbly, doubled, and smells pleasantly tangy, it will do the same job. The levain build is about timing and quantity, not magic.
faqs.question: Can I just use my starter instead of building a levain?

faqs.answer: Use it at its peak, when it has domed and is full of bubbles. A levain that has risen and fallen back is past its best: it will still leaven, but the bread will be more sour and the rise slower. If it has fallen, feed it once more and use it at the next peak.
faqs.question: What if my levain peaks before I am ready to mix?

faqs.answer: About 10 to 20 g extra, to cover what sticks to the jar and the spoon. If the recipe needs 200 g, build 220 g. The calculator works for any target weight, so type 220 and it will split it for you.
faqs.question: Should I build more levain than the recipe needs?

felicityNote: I build my levain the night before, at 1:5:5, and it is waiting for me in the morning like it set an alarm. The slow build is the easiest schedule I have found.

parts.meaning: The total levain weight your recipe needs, in grams. This is the number you start from.
Starter, flour, and water by weight. At 1:2:2 the total is 5 parts; at 1:5:5 it is 11 parts.
The ripe starter from your jar. At 1:2:2 it is one fifth of the total levain.
Fresh flour for the build. At 1:2:2 it is two fifths of the total levain.
Fresh water for the build. Always the same weight as the flour, so the levain stays at 100% hydration.

formula.text: Parts = 1 + flour parts + water parts. Seed starter = levain ÷ parts. Flour = seed starter × flour parts. Water = seed starter × water parts.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the seed starter
howToSteps.text: Put a clean jar on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the seed starter from the calculator. A tablespoon or two of ripe starter is usually enough.

howToSteps.name: Add the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Weigh in the flour and water from the calculator. Stir until no dry flour is left, scrape down the sides, and mark the level with a rubber band.

howToSteps.name: Leave it to ripen
howToSteps.text: Cover loosely and leave at room temperature. A 1:1:1 build ripens in a few hours, a 1:2:2 build in about 5 hours at 74 to 76°F, and a 1:5:5 build overnight.

howToSteps.name: Use it at its peak
howToSteps.text: The levain is ready when it has domed, is full of bubbles, and smells pleasantly tangy. Mix it into the dough at its peak, not after it has fallen back.

title: Sourdough Levain Builder Calculator
tutorial: A levain is a small batch of starter built for one bake. Your starter is the culture you keep alive in the jar, week after week. A levain is a spoonful of that starter, fed fresh flour and water, and left to ripen into exactly the amount the recipe needs. The starter stays in the jar, the levain goes in the dough, and you never have to keep a huge jar of starter just to bake one loaf.

The maths starts from the target weight and works backwards. A 1:2:2 build has five parts in total: one part starter, two parts flour, two parts water. For 200 g of levain, each part is 40 g, so you need 40 g of starter, 80 g of flour, and 80 g of water. A 1:5:5 build has eleven parts, so 150 g of levain needs 14 g of starter, 68 g of flour, and 68 g of water. The flour and water are always equal, which keeps the levain at 100% hydration.

The ratio sets the timing. A 1:1:1 build ripens fastest, in a few hours in a warm kitchen, and it is the right choice when you decide to bake in the morning and want dough by lunch. The Perfect Loaf's levain builds at 1:2:2 ripen in about 5 hours at 74 to 76°F, which is a useful guide for a same-day bake. A 1:5:5 build is the slow one: mix it in the evening and it is ready in the morning, which is the easiest schedule I have found.

Build a little more than the recipe needs, about 10 to 20 g extra, to cover what sticks to the jar and the spoon. If the recipe needs 200 g, build 220 g. The calculator works for any target weight, so type 220 and it will split it for you. The extra levain is also a safety net: if you spill a little, you still have enough.

Use the levain at its peak, when it has domed and is full of bubbles and smells pleasantly tangy. A levain that has risen and fallen back is past its best. It will still leaven, but the bread will be more sour and the rise slower. If your levain peaks before you are ready to mix, put it in the fridge to slow it down, or feed it once more and use it at the next peak.
